title: Objection: 'Eternal Life, Eternal Punishment'
hook: If the punishment ends, doesn't eternal life end too?
tldr: Matthew 25:46 uses one Greek word, aionios, for both punishment and life. Since Augustine, traditionalists have argued that both must therefore be endless. The parallel is real, but the word basically means 'of the age to come'. It can describe either a lasting result or a limited stretch of time, so the verse alone cannot prove endless conscious torment.
big_idea: One shared adjective does not settle what the punishment is.

points.title: The parallel is real
points.text: Both clauses use aionios. Traditionalists, from Augustine to modern Reformed writers, say the two must last equally long. Opponents of eternal torment mostly accept the parallel but dispute what aionios means.

points.title: Aionios means 'of the age'
points.text: The adjective comes from aion, 'age'. In the Bible it often describes the age to come. Context shows whether a long, bounded time or an endless one is meant.

points.title: Aidios was the stronger word
points.text: Ramelli and Konstan note that Greek had a stronger word for endlessness, aidios. The New Testament uses it only twice, and never for the punishment of human beings.

points.title: Eternal result, not endless process
points.text: Conditionalists point out that 'eternal fire' destroyed Sodom once and for all, and the fire is no longer burning. Likewise, 'eternal punishment' can mean a destruction whose result is never reversed.

points.title: Kolasis leans toward correction
points.text: Aristotle distinguished kolasis, punishment for the sufferer's good, from timoria, punishment that satisfies the punisher. Matthew 25:46 uses kolasis, though even Hart admits the word alone cannot settle the question.

points.title: Life's endlessness rests elsewhere
points.text: Believers' endless life does not depend on one adjective. Scripture says the risen cannot die and that mortality puts on immortality.

sections.summary: In City of God book 21, Augustine argued that 'eternal' cannot mean endless for life and temporary for punishment within the same sentence. Both must last equally long. Robert Peterson's Hell on Trial, The Gospel Coalition, GTY and Equip all repeat the argument: Jesus gives both fates the same adjective, so if the life never ends, neither does the punishment.

Aionios is the adjective of aion, 'age'. The Greek Old Testament usually translates the Hebrew olam with aion or aionios. Olam can mark a bounded time. A slave serves his master 'forever', meaning for life (Exodus 21:6). Jonah was shut in 'forever', yet he spent three days in the fish (Jonah 2:6). Even Ellicott's commentary said the word does not in itself mean endlessness.

sections.h: One word, two senses, two verses
sections.summary: Romans 16:25-26 uses aionios twice in a row. A mystery kept secret through 'times eternal' (chronois aioniois), which many translations render 'long ages past', has now been revealed by command of the 'eternal God'. The first use has an end point, which is now. The second refers to God. The word's force depends on what it describes.

sections.h: Aidios: the word Jesus did not use
sections.summary: Ilaria Ramelli and David Konstan's study Terms for Eternity traces aionios and aidios from Plato through the church fathers. Aidios carries the strong sense of everlasting. In the New Testament it appears only in Romans 1:20, for God's eternal power, and Jude 6, where the angels' 'everlasting chains' last only 'until the judgment'. Ramelli observes that patristic universalists used aidios for life but never for punishment.

Aristotle (Rhetoric 1.10) says kolasis is for the sake of the one who suffers it, while timoria satisfies the one who inflicts it. Barclay and Thayer note that the root verb first meant pruning trees. David Bentley Hart translates the verse: 'the chastening of that Age… the life of that Age.' Traditionalists answer that BDAG defines kolasis here as 'transcendent retribution', and that Jewish writings of the period used it for penalties.

sections.h: Three ways to keep the parallel
sections.summary: Readers who reject eternal torment do not all deny the parallel. Conditionalists such as Rethinking Hell say the punishment is as permanent as the life, but it is destruction, as in 'eternal destruction' (2 Thessalonians 1:9). Universalists such as Hart and Ramelli read both clauses as 'of the age to come'. On that view, the life's endlessness is taught elsewhere and the chastening can end.

Traditionalists respond that the age-based gloss is 'imposed' on Matthew 25:46 (Crosswalk), and that GTY sees no good exegetical reason to make 'eternal' a quality rather than a duration. Michael McClymond, reviewing Hart, grants that aionios occasionally means 'age-long'. He still calls Hart's consistent 'age' rendering woodenly rigid. Ron Rhodes adds that Scripture teaches degrees of punishment, which simple annihilation does not fit.

notes.note: Greek kolasin aionion. Hart renders it 'the chastening of that Age'; traditionalists render it 'everlasting punishment'.
Kolasis: Aristotle defines it as punishment for the sufferer's sake, unlike timoria. BDAG instead glosses it here as 'transcendent retribution'.
Zoen aionion, 'life of the age to come'. Its endlessness is also taught in Luke 20:36 and 1 Corinthians 15:53.

visuals.caption: The same adjective appears in both halves. The debate is over what that adjective tells us.

items.meaning: Long or unseen duration. It is used for a slave's lifetime service (Exodus 21:6) and for Jonah's three days in the fish (Jonah 2:6).
The adjective of aion. It describes the age to come and things belonging to it. Its length depends on what it describes.
The stronger word for endlessness. In the New Testament it is used only for God's power and for angelic chains that last 'until the judgment'.
Punishment. Aristotle used it for punishment aimed at the sufferer's good. It appears only in Matthew 25:46 and 1 John 4:18.
Punishment that satisfies the one who inflicts it. Jesus does not use this word in Matthew 25:46.

children.label: Eternal conscious torment
children.note: Endless duration of suffering, matching endless life (Augustine, Peterson, Burk).

children.label: Conditional immortality
children.note: Endless result: a destruction that is never reversed (Fudge, Rethinking Hell).

children.label: Restoration
children.note: The corrective chastening of the coming age, which can end (Hart, Ramelli).

mythfact.myth: Aionios always means 'without end' in Greek.
mythfact.fact: Even traditional commentators like Ellicott said the word does not in itself mean endlessness. Romans 16:25 uses it for ages that have now ended.

mythfact.myth: Only universalists question the parallelism argument.
mythfact.fact: Conditionalists accept that the punishment is permanent but read it as permanent destruction. Universalists read both clauses as 'of the age to come'. Their reasons differ.

mythfact.myth: Kolasis proves the punishment is corrective.
mythfact.fact: Aristotle's definition supports a corrective sense, but Hart himself concedes the exact meaning in Matthew 25:46 cannot be pinned down. The stronger arguments concern aionios.

terms.meaning: Augustine's claim that one adjective in one sentence must give life and punishment the same endless duration.
Greek adjective from aion, 'age'. It means belonging to an age, especially the age to come. Endlessness depends on context.
Greek word for perpetual or everlasting. The New Testament uses it only in Romans 1:20 and Jude 6.
Punishment. In Aristotle's usage it is aimed at correcting the one punished. It originally meant pruning.
Retributive punishment that satisfies the one who inflicts it.

quotes.text: Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.

verses.role: The key text. The same adjective, aionios, describes both the punishment and the life.
Aionios describes ages that have now ended and also the eternal God, in back-to-back verses.
A slave serves his master 'forever', meaning for life.
Jonah was barred in 'forever', yet only for three days.
Sodom suffers 'eternal fire': the fire went out, but the destruction is permanent.
Aidios chains last only 'until the judgment of the great day'.
'Eternal destruction': conditionalists read aionios punishment as a lasting result.
The resurrected 'can no longer die'. Endless life is grounded here, not only in aionios.
The only other New Testament use of kolasis: fear has to do with punishment.

quiz.q: Which church father made the parallelism argument from Matthew 25:46 famous?
quiz.why: In City of God book 21, Augustine argued that 'eternal' must mean the same thing for life and for punishment in one sentence.

quiz.q: Which Greek word for 'everlasting' is never used in the New Testament for human punishment?
quiz.why: Aidios appears only in Romans 1:20 and Jude 6. Ramelli and Konstan argue this choice of vocabulary is significant.

quiz.q: How do conditionalists keep the parallel in Matthew 25:46?
options: They deny the verse is authentic
They say the punishment is a permanent destruction
They say the life also ends
quiz.why: Like Sodom's 'eternal fire' in Jude 7, the punishment's result lasts forever even though the process does not.

reflect: Should one shared adjective outweigh what the rest of Scripture says about God's purposes in judgment?

objections.claim: The same word describes life and punishment in one sentence. If the punishment ends, so does eternal life.
objections.strongest: Augustine: within one breath, Jesus cannot mean 'endless' for one clause and 'temporary' for the other. The parallel is deliberate and antithetical. Weakening the punishment weakens the believer's hope, since the two stand or fall together.
objections.response: The parallel is real, but it shows only that both belong to the same age. It does not show what each one is. Conditionalists accept equal permanence: the life never ends, and the destruction is never undone. Universalists read both as 'of the age to come' and ground endless life in other texts, which say the risen cannot die and the mortal puts on immortality. Romans 16:25-26 shows aionios in two neighbouring verses with different ranges: past ages that ended, and the eternal God. The adjective takes its force from its subject.

objections.claim: Standard lexicons define aionios as 'without beginning or end'. Age-based readings are special pleading invented to avoid hell.
objections.strongest: Thayer and BDAG list 'eternal' as the main New Testament sense. The phrase 'pertaining to the age to come' is an imposed gloss (Crosswalk). Translators across centuries and traditions have rendered Matthew 25:46 'everlasting'.
objections.response: No one denies that aionios can describe endless things. The question is whether it must. The Greek Old Testament uses aion and aionios for the Hebrew olam, which covers a slave's lifetime (Exodus 21:6) and Jonah's three days (Jonah 2:6). Romans 16:25 uses it for ages now past, and the KJV renders that 'since the world began'. Even Ellicott said the word does not in itself involve endlessness. McClymond, Hart's sharpest critic, grants that it occasionally means 'age-long'. So the lexicon leaves the question to context.

objections.claim: Kolasis in Jesus' day meant retributive penalty, so Aristotle's 'corrective' definition is irrelevant.
objections.strongest: BDAG glosses kolasis in Matthew 25:46 as 'transcendent retribution'. Intertestamental Jewish texts use it for penalties imposed for wrongdoing. Aristotle's distinction was a philosopher's definition, not a rule of everyday Greek four centuries later.
objections.response: This objection has real force, and fair-minded restorationists concede part of it. Hart says the precise meaning of kolasis in Matthew 25:46 cannot be pinned down. Still, the word's root sense is pruning. Aristotle's distinction was known, and church fathers used kolasis for corrective discipline. Jesus also chose kolasis, not timoria. Even if kolasis here means retribution, its duration still depends on aionios. A retributive penalty can be proportionate and finite. So the case against endless torment does not rest on kolasis.

objections.claim: If aionios can mean temporary, then the 'eternal God' and 'eternal Spirit' might not be eternal either.
objections.strongest: Any reading that makes aionios bounded for punishment must explain why it is unbounded for God (Romans 16:26) and the Spirit (Hebrews 9:14). Otherwise the argument proves too much and dissolves the language of everlasting glory.
objections.response: God is endless because of who God is, not because of one adjective. Scripture says this with other words: God alone has immortality (1 Timothy 6:16), and Paul uses aidios for God's power (Romans 1:20). Aionios describes what belongs to the coming age, and God is the source of that age. That is why an aionios thing tied to God is endless, while an aionios hill (Genesis 49:26) or slave service is not. Context decides, which is exactly what the anti-ECT reading claims.

objections.claim: Jude 7 says Sodom is presently 'undergoing' the punishment of eternal fire. That is conscious, ongoing suffering.
objections.strongest: CARM notes the present participle in Jude 7: Sodom's people are now suffering eternal fire. If that is so, the 'example' teaches continuing conscious punishment, and aionios fire in Matthew 25:41 is the same unending fire.
objections.response: Jude says Sodom 'serves as an example'. The visible example was the burnt-out cities, which 2 Peter 2:6 says were reduced to ashes. That fire is not burning today. Fudge, and commentator Richard Bauckham, note that the lasting desolation shows the destruction is permanent. Jesus even said it would be 'more tolerable' for Sodom at the judgment (Matthew 11:24), and Ezekiel 16:53-55 foresees Sodom's fortunes restored. So 'eternal fire' describes fire from the coming age with a permanent result, not flames that never go out.

objections.claim: Hart and Ramelli are revisionists. The consensus of scholars and translators reads Matthew 25:46 as everlasting torment.
objections.strongest: Michael McClymond argues that Hart's 'age' rendering is woodenly and foolishly rigid, and that Ramelli's reading of the fathers is selective. Majority scholarship, not a few brilliant outliers, should govern how we read Jesus.
objections.response: McClymond's critique targets Hart's rigid consistency. It does not show that aionios always means endless, which McClymond himself denies. Ramelli and Konstan's study was published in a scholarly series, reviewed in Bryn Mawr Classical Review, and answered its critics there. Long before Hart, Greek-speaking fathers who knew the language natively read aionios punishment as non-endless; see the topic on church history. Majority opinion matters, but the argument has to be settled by the evidence of usage.

objections.claim: Questioning 'eternal' undermines Christians' assurance that their life with God will never end.
objections.strongest: Believers cling to 'eternal life' as a promise. If Jesus' words can be re-read as 'age-long', grieving and dying Christians lose their certainty, and the gospel's promise becomes negotiable.
objections.response: Assurance never rested on a single adjective. Jesus says those who believe 'will never die' (John 11:26). The resurrected 'can no longer die' (Luke 20:36). Christ lives by 'the power of an indestructible life' (Hebrews 7:16). Believers' hope is anchored in the risen Christ, and none of these texts depends on how aionios is read in Matthew 25:46. Reading the punishment more carefully does not weaken that promise.
